theme: Micah’s idol; the Danites, religion as private property
readingInstruction: Read Judges 17:1-18:31. These chapters begin the long appendix to the book of Judges, which shows how deeply Israel has fallen. Watch for the repeated phrase, “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” Notice how religion becomes a personal convenience.
settingTheScene: The stories of the judges are over, but the book is not. The last five chapters tell two stories that illustrate the moral and spiritual collapse of the nation. The first, which you read today, is about a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim, his stolen silver, his private shrine, and a wandering Levite who is hired as his priest. The tribe of Dan then passes through, steals the idol and the priest, and conquers a peaceful city. The two stories show religion without God, worship shaped to the worshiper’s tastes, and a priesthood for hire. They are told with dry irony, and they explain why the book keeps saying that Israel needed a king.
observation: Micah’s mother has 1,100 pieces of silver stolen, and she pronounces a curse. When Micah confesses, she blesses him in the LORD’s name (17:1-2).
She dedicates the silver to the LORD to make an idol, and Micah sets up a shrine with an ephod and household gods (17:3-5).
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6).
A young Levite from Bethlehem, looking for a place to live, agrees to be Micah’s priest for ten pieces of silver a year (17:7-12).
Micah says, “Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest” (17:13).
The tribe of Dan, looking for land, sends spies, who consult the Levite and are told, “Your journey is under the eye of the LORD” (18:5-6).
The Danites steal Micah’s idols and persuade the Levite to come with them: “Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe?” (18:19).
They destroy the peaceful city of Laish, rename it Dan, and set up the idol for themselves (18:27-31).
The author notes that the idol was there “all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh” (18:31).
interpretation:
The Micah story is a careful satire. It begins with a theft and a curse, and the thief is the man’s own son. The mother then blesses him in the LORD’s name and dedicates the silver to the LORD, and promptly uses part of it to make an idol. Everything is mixed up. They use the name of the LORD, but they ignore his law. They speak of dedication, but they violate the second commandment. The household is spiritually confused, and nobody notices.

Micah’s shrine is a religion of convenience. He has his own ephod, his own household gods, and his own priest. He even ordains his son. When a Levite from Bethlehem wanders by, Micah hires him, believing that he now has God’s favor secured: “Now I know that the LORD will prosper me.” He thinks he can buy blessing. The Levite, a man who should have been serving at the tabernacle and teaching the law, takes the job for ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes. The point is that even those whose calling is to teach God’s word have drifted.

The Danites arrive and complete the picture. They seek an inheritance, not trusting God to give them the land he had allotted. They consult the Levite, who gives a vague blessing: “Your journey is under the eye of the LORD.” It is exactly what they want to hear. Then they take Micah’s idol and the priest. When Micah protests, they threaten him. The Levite goes with them gladly. He finds the offer of a tribe more attractive than a household. His loyalty is to his own advancement.

The conquest of Laish makes the point. They attack a quiet city with no allies, “a people quiet and unsuspecting,” and burn it. They then set up the idol and appoint the priest. The narrator adds a quiet closing note: all this happened while God’s house was at Shiloh. The true worship was available, and they ignored it.

The whole story shows religion as private property. Each person designs his own faith. What is right in his own eyes becomes the standard, and even the name of the LORD is attached to it. This is not an ancient problem. It is the habit of our day: faith shaped to personal taste, clergy chosen by what they offer, and worship tuned to what feels right. The corrective is the word of God and a true king. Only Christ is the true priest and king, who cannot be bought and who does not tell us only what we want to hear.
connection: The second commandment is in Exodus 20:4-6. The Levites’ calling is in Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 33:8-10. Dan’s later role as one of the places where Jeroboam set up a golden calf appears in 1 Kings 12:28-30. The “no king” refrain recurs in Judges 18:1, 19:1, and 21:25. Compare the false teachers who say what people want to hear in 2 Timothy 4:3-4. Christ as the true priest and king appears in Hebrews 7.
application:
Test your own faith for “Micah’s shrine.” Are there areas where you have designed God to suit your preferences, such as a convenient view of sin, a comfortable church, or a vague spirituality? Ask the Lord to correct them with his word.

Think about who shapes your beliefs. Do you listen to those who tell you what you want to hear, or to those who tell you the truth? Seek out one person who will speak honestly.

Finally, thank God for the true priest who cannot be hired and the true king who rules in righteousness.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have shaped God to your tastes.
Ask him to teach you to worship him as he is, in spirit and truth.
